statement: Twelve numbers are written around a circle. Each number is equal to the average of its two neighbours. One of the numbers is 7. What is the sum of all twelve numbers?

choices.misconception: I gave the value of the number I was told about instead of the sum of all twelve.
I added up the sums of each number's two neighbours, which are 14 at every one of the twelve places.
I added each number together with its two neighbours, 21 at every one of the twelve places.
I thought knowing one number leaves the other eleven free to vary.

hints: Look at the largest of the twelve numbers.
Use the extremal principle: take the biggest number. It is the average of its neighbours, and neither neighbour is bigger. Ask what that forces, then keep going around the circle.
If the largest number M is the average of two numbers that are each at most M, both of them must equal M.

solutions.reliable: Let M be the largest of the twelve numbers. M is the average of its two neighbours, and neither neighbour exceeds M, so both must equal M; otherwise their average would be less than M. The same argument then applies to each neighbour, and walking around the circle shows that every number equals M. Since one of them is 7, all twelve are 7 and the sum is 12 x 7 = 84. The transferable idea: look at the largest or smallest element, which is where a constraint bites hardest.
solutions.elegant: Being the average of its neighbours means each number exceeds the one before it by the same amount as the next exceeds it, so the numbers go up by a constant step around the circle. Twelve steps return to the start, so the step is 0 and all twelve numbers are equal.

whyOnTest: Many unknowns and one fact look underdetermined, but looking at the largest number forces every number to be equal.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
